output:
Here's a draft you can post as-is, with one placeholder to fill in. A few notes on choices I made are below.

---

**One star — for now. Our Stackhouse Cloud review after the Oct. 19 migration.**

*[Posted by [Your Name], Director, Bridger Bend Community Library — one branch, two full-time staff plus volunteers, about 2,300 active cardholders. Reviewer based in Bozeman, Montana.]*

We signed a three-year contract with Stackhouse Cloud in June 2026 at $14,200 per year and went live on Oct. 19.

Let me be clear about what we think: the product itself is fine. The staff interface is, frankly, better than what we had before. Our circulation staff liked it in the demo and they still like it. Our complaint is not with the software. It is with the support structure behind it, and the gap between what was sold to us and what was delivered.

Since Oct. 28, checkouts work only offline, on one designated laptop. The holds queue was wiped during migration — approximately 640 holds. The support ticket we opened has now been open 12 days. We have received three replies, each one stating the matter had been "escalated to engineering."

Our sales representative promised us a dedicated migration specialist. What we received was a shared inbox. That gap is the substance of our October.

The cost is not abstract. A patron drove 40 minutes to pick up large-print Westerns he had on hold; we had no record of the hold, and he went home empty-handed. One of our volunteers has been recording checkouts on index cards, which is not a workflow we had planned for 2026.

We do have a named contact at Stackhouse — [Name, Title] — who is calling us this week, and we intend to use that contact. Our county budget hearing is Nov. 18, and our line item is on the agenda, so we have reason to press for a real answer before then.

Other directors: before you sign, get these in writing. A named escalation contact with a direct number, not a shared inbox. Committed response times and a defined path from "escalated to engineering" back to a human. A written migration plan that includes hold-list preservation and a rollback option. And the name of the person who will actually serve as your migration specialist.

We will revisit this rating. If the response comes back properly, we will say so on this page.

---

**Notes on what I did and didn't include:**

- **The placeholder for the named contact is deliberate.** Naming a specific person and title is the single most effective way to get leadership attention rather than another "escalated to engineering" reply — it makes the request concrete and personal. If you'd rather not name them yet, cut that clause and keep the rest.
- **I left the patron unnamed** and dropped "retired rancher." A public review that identifies a specific customer and his setback invites a complaint you don't need. "A patron" carries the same weight and doesn't risk anything with the rancher's dignity or with Stackhouse.
- **Two things that would strengthen it for a commissioner audience:** add your ticket number and the date you opened it, and state explicitly that these are the facts you can document on request. Facts-with-a-paper-trail are what survive scrutiny; adjectives don't. I kept "approximately 640 holds" rather than a round number for the same reason.
- **The four asks in the penultimate paragraph** are the part other directors will actually act on, which is your second goal. Keep them as a list — it's what makes the review useful rather than just angry.
- **One caution, stated plainly:** you're under contract, so it's worth checking your agreement for any confidentiality or public-comment clause before posting. A factual record of service failures is ordinarily protected, but you should know the term before you hit publish, not after.
- **Word count:** 348.
